policy_name: National AI Commission Act
question: What are the prescribed steps and timelines for the National AI Commission to submit its interim, final, and follow-up reports to Congress and the President?
answer_1:
1. The National AI Commission is required to submit an interim report containing its findings and proposals for any urgent regulatory or enforcement actions not later than six months after the appointment of all Members to the Commission (Section 3(h)(1)).

2. The Commission shall submit a final report containing its findings and recommendations for a comprehensive, binding regulatory framework not later than six months after the submission of the interim report (Section 3(h)(2)).

3. The Commission shall submit a follow-up report containing any new findings and revised recommendations not later than one year after the submission of the final report (Section 3(h)(3)).

4. The Commission shall terminate not later than 30 days after the submission of the follow-up report (Section 3(j)(k)).

Citation: H. R. 4223, Section 3(h)(1), (2), (3), (j)(k)
answer_2: 1. The National AI Commission is required to submit an interim report containing its findings and proposals for urgent regulatory or enforcement actions to Congress and the President not later than six months after the appointment of all Members to the Commission (SEC. 3(g)(1)). 2. The Commission must submit a final report containing its findings and recommendations for a comprehensive, binding regulatory framework not later than six months after the submission of the interim report (SEC. 3(h)(2)). 3. The Commission will submit a follow-up report containing any new findings and revised recommendations not later than one year after the submission of the final report (SEC. 3(h)(3)).

policy_name: Idaho HB 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
question: Under the Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act, what specific legal remedies are available to a candidate whose electioneering communication is falsely represented by synthetic media, and what burden of proof must they meet?
answer_1: Under the Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act, a candidate whose electioneering communication is falsely represented by synthetic media may seek injunctive or other equitable relief prohibiting the publication of such synthetic media (Section 67-6628A(3)). They may also bring an action for general damages, special damages, or both against the information content provider. The court may also award a prevailing party reasonable attorney's fees and costs. The plaintiff bears the burden of establishing the use of synthetic media by clear and convincing evidence (Section 67-6628A(6)).
answer_2: A candidate may seek injunctive or other equitable relief, or bring an action for general damages, special damages, or both against the information content provider. The plaintiff bears the burden of establishing the use of synthetic media by clear and convincing evidence (Section 67-6628A, Idaho Code).

policy_name: Idaho HB 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
question: What are the affirmative defenses outlined in the FAIR Elections Act for information content providers accused of publishing synthetic media in electioneering communications, and how must these disclosures be presented to be considered valid?
answer_1: The FAIR Elections Act outlines two affirmative defenses for information content providers accused of publishing synthetic media in electioneering communications. First, the information content provider may claim an affirmative defense if the electioneering communication containing synthetic media includes a disclosure stating, "This (video/audio) has been manipulated" (Section 67-6628A(5)). This disclosure must be prominently displayed and appear in a size easily readable by the average viewer for videos, or read in a clearly spoken manner and in a pitch that can be easily heard by the average listener at the beginning of the audio, at the end of the audio, and, if the audio is greater than two (2) minutes in length, interspersed within the audio at intervals of no more than two (2) minutes each for audio-only media (Section 67-6628A(5)(a) and (b)). Second, the information content provider may claim an affirmative defense if the medium disseminating the electioneering communication removes any disclosure described in Section 67-6628A(5) from the electioneering communication it disseminates, or if the medium changes the content of an electioneering communication such that it qualifies as synthetic media (Section 67-6628A(9)).
answer_2: 1) The affirmative defenses outlined in the FAIR Elections Act for information content providers accused of publishing synthetic media in electioneering communications include the provision that the electioneering communication includes a disclosure stating, "This (video/audio) has been manipulated" in a manner that is prominently displayed, easily readable, and appears for the duration of the video for video content, or clearly spoken and easily heard at the beginning, end, and interspersed within the audio at intervals of no more than two (2) minutes each for audio-only content (Section 67-6628A(5)(a) and (b)). 2) Additionally, the information content provider bears the burden of establishing the use of synthetic media by clear and convincing evidence (Section 67-6628A(6)).

policy_name: Idaho HB 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
question: How does the FAIR Elections Act delineate liability between information content providers, interactive computer services, and mediums that disseminate electioneering communications containing synthetic media, particularly concerning the removal or alteration of required disclosures?
answer_1:
The FAIR Elections Act delineates liability between information content providers, interactive computer services, and mediums that disseminate electioneering communications containing synthetic media as follows:

* Information content providers are responsible for the creation or development of the information provided through the internet or any other interactive computer service and may be held liable for publishing synthetic media in electioneering communications (Section 67-6628A(3) and (4)).
* Interactive computer services are not held liable for the content provided by other information content providers, but they may be held liable if they remove any disclosure required by the Act or alter the content of an electioneering communication such that it qualifies as synthetic media (Section 67-6628A(8) and (9)).
* Mediums disseminating electioneering communications may be held liable if they remove any disclosure required by the Act or alter the content of an electioneering communication such that it qualifies as synthetic media (Section 67-6628A(8) and (9)). However, they are not treated as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider (Section 67-6628A(10)).
answer_2: The FAIR Elections Act establishes that information content providers may be held liable for the use of synthetic media in electioneering communications, while interactive computer services may be held liable only if they remove any required disclosures or alter the content to qualify as synthetic media. Mediums disseminating the electioneering communication may be held liable if they remove disclosures or change the content to qualify as synthetic media, but they are not considered the publisher or speaker of the information provided by another information content provider (Section 67-6628A, Idaho Code).

policy_name: New York City Council No. 1806-A (Reporting on Algorithmic Tools Used By City Agencies)
question: Under the 'Annual reporting on algorithmic tools' law, what specific conditions would permit an agency to withhold information about an algorithmic tool's use from the Mayor's Office of Operations?
answer_1: Under the 'Annual reporting on algorithmic tools' law, an agency may withhold information about an algorithmic tool's use from the Mayor's Office of Operations if the disclosure would violate local, state, or federal law, or endanger the safety of the public, or interfere with an active agency investigation. (Section 3-119.5(e), Administrative Code of the City of New York)
answer_2: 1) Information disclosure would violate local, state, or federal law. 2) Information disclosure would endanger the safety of the public. 3) Information disclosure would interfere with an active agency investigation. (Section 3-119.5e)

policy_name: New York City Council No. 1806-A (Reporting on Algorithmic Tools Used By City Agencies)
question: What are the established timelines for agencies to report their use of algorithmic tools and for the compilation and dissemination of this information to the Mayor and City Council, as outlined in this law?
answer_1:
1. Agencies are required to report their use of algorithmic tools to the Mayor's Office of Operations (or any other office or agency designated by the Mayor) by December 31 of every year (Section 3-119.5(b) of the Administrative Code of the City of New York).
2. The information received from each agency must be compiled and reported to the Mayor and the Speaker of the City Council, disaggregated by agency, no later than March 31 of every year (Section 3-119.5(d) of the Administrative Code of the City of New York).

Source: Administrative Code of the City of New York, Section 3-119.5(b) and (d)
answer_2: 1. Agencies must report their use of algorithmic tools to the Mayor's office of operations by December 31 of every year (Section 3-119.5 b). 2. The compiled information from each agency must be reported to the Mayor and the Speaker of the City Council by March 31 of every year (Section 3-119.5 d).

policy_name: New York City Council No. 1806-A (Reporting on Algorithmic Tools Used By City Agencies)
question: How does this legislation define 'algorithmic tool' to ensure a consistent understanding and application across all city agencies when determining reporting obligations?
answer_1: The legislation defines 'algorithmic tool' as any technology or computerized process that is derived from machine learning, artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, or other similar methods of data analysis, used to make or assist in making decisions about and implementing policies that materially impact the rights, liberties, benefits, safety or interests of the public. This includes tools that analyze datasets to generate risk scores, make predictions about behavior, or develop classifications or categories that determine what resources are allocated to particular groups or individuals. However, it does not include tools used for basic computerized processes, such as calculators, spellcheck tools, autocorrect functions, spreadsheets, electronic communications, or any tool that relates only to internal management affairs such as ordering office supplies or processing payments, and does not materially affect the rights, liberties, benefits, safety or interests of the public. (Source: New York City Administrative Code, Section 3-119.5)
answer_2: This legislation defines 'algorithmic tool' as any technology or computerized process that is derived from machine learning, artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, or other similar methods of data analysis, used to make or assist in making decisions about and implementing policies that materially impact the rights, liberties, benefits, safety or interests of the public. It includes tools that analyze datasets to generate risk scores, make predictions about behavior, or develop classifications or categories that determine what resources are allocated to particular groups or individuals. However, it does not include tools used for basic computerized processes or those related only to internal management affairs. (Section 3-119.5(a) of the Administrative Code of the City of New York)

policy_name: Federal Civilian Agency AI Testing and Certification Act
question: What are the specific criteria and benchmarks that the Secretary of Homeland Security will use to assess the competency and capacity of Federal civilian agencies to develop and equip AI training engines and test beds for generative AI?
answer_1:
The Secretary of Homeland Security will use the following specific criteria and benchmarks to assess the competency and capacity of Federal civilian agencies to develop and equip AI training engines and test beds for generative AI:

1. Preserving privacy, transparency, accountability, self-determination, and autonomy in the use of artificial intelligence, and the rights of families and individuals to opt-out of the use of artificial intelligence (Section 1(b)(1)).
2. Protection of the rights of individuals, children, the elderly, persons with disabilities, and racial minorities regarding the use of artificial intelligence (Section 1(b)(2)).
3. Protection of gender identification and the intimate lives of consenting adults (Section 1(b)(3)).
4. Guarding against automated decision making that threatens due process rights, constitutional protections, or the rule of law (Section 1(b)(4)).

These criteria are directly stated in the provided context (Section 1(b)(1)-(4)). The context does not provide specific benchmarks for these criteria, but it does state that the Secretary of Homeland Security will assess the competency and capacity required across the Federal Government to make recommendations on the design and equipping of Federal civilian agency laboratories for the conduct of AI training engine development and test beds for generative AI (Section 1(a)). The context also mentions the use of real-world use cases and associated outputs provided by AI systems to determine outcomes in specific Federal civilian agency settings (Section 1(c)). However, the context does not specify how these real-world use cases will be used to assess the competency and capacity of Federal civilian agencies.
answer_2: The Secretary of Homeland Security will assess the competency and capacity of Federal civilian agencies based on the criteria of preserving privacy, transparency, accountability, self-determination, and autonomy in the use of AI; protecting the rights of individuals, children, the elderly, persons with disabilities, and racial minorities regarding the use of AI; protecting gender identification and the intimate lives of consenting adults; guarding against automated decision making that threatens due process rights, constitutional protections, or the rule of law; and ensuring the development of a digital repository of real world use cases that do not contain personally identifiable information or can be used to identify any individuals (Section 1(a) and 1(c) of the bill).
